title: The Skill of Making Decisions
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: A California gourmet store set out twenty-four flavors of jam for tasting: crowds stopped, but barely one in thirty of the people who looked actually bought anything. With six flavors, nearly one in three bought, ten times as many. Contrary to what our world believes, too many options don’t set us free. They paralyze us, drive up our expectations, and rob us of joy even in a good choice, because all the rejected possibilities keep hovering in the background.

Researchers have described two kinds of people. The maximizer has to find the best possible option: comparing, going back, checking again. The skilled chooser settles on criteria in advance and takes the first thing that meets them. The findings are counterintuitive: maximizers choose slightly better, yet they are clearly less satisfied and have more regrets. “Good enough” isn’t surrender. It’s wisdom.

When it matters, watch four things. Widen the frame: the question “Change jobs or stay?” hides renegotiating your terms, switching fields, or going part-time; ask yourself what you would do if this option didn’t exist. Look for arguments against your own leaning, because the heart collects only the arguments in favor. Test the distance: how will you see this in ten days, ten months, and ten years? And leave a margin for error, but don’t hide in putting things off: a decision not made is still a decision, only one made by circumstances, and people at the end of life regret the things they didn’t do more often than the things they did. Add to that a rule of pace: make reversible decisions quickly, because endless hesitation costs more than a mistake, and irreversible ones slowly, with reflection and counsel. Once you’ve decided, stop comparing. And put the small stuff on autopilot: a set weekly menu, a set shopping list, a set route. The mind gets tired from deciding, which is why in the evening, after hundreds of micro-choices, impulsive decisions come so easily. And a compass of values, settled once, will lift hundreds of dilemmas off your shoulders, because most decisions will then make themselves.

Young Solomon didn’t ask for riches but for an understanding heart to judge wisely. The Bible treats wisdom not as a talent but as a gift we are free to ask for, and it adds a liberating truth: a person’s worth doesn’t depend on how well they choose. Whoever knows this decides with a calmer heart.

quote.text: Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him.

questions: Which unmade decision has been waiting on you the longest, and what is putting it off costing you?
Do you have a compass of values you settled once, or do you decide every matter from scratch?

paragraphs: A gourmet store in California once set up a jam-tasting booth. When twenty-four flavors were on display, crowds stopped at the booth, but barely one customer in thirty went to the register with a jar. When there were only six flavors, fewer people stopped, but nearly one in three bought, ten times as many. This simple experiment challenged something the Western world believes as a given: the more choice, the better. It turns out that past a certain threshold, extra options don’t add freedom. They add weight.

And we live in an age of record weight. Our grandparents chose between two kinds of cheese and one career path, usually laid out by the family they grew up in. We choose among dozens of breakfast cereals, hundreds of phone models, thousands of TV series, and countless ways to live: where to settle, what to study, when to commit and to whom. Each of these possibilities, taken on its own, is a blessing. All of them together create a state psychologists call decision paralysis: the mind would rather not decide at all than risk choosing the forty-seventh of three hundred options instead of the best one. A second mechanism is sneakier still: the more options we have looked through, the higher our expectations climb and the easier it is to be disappointed even by a good choice, because all the rejected possibilities keep hovering in the background. And a third: a new thing brings joy for a shorter time than it promised, because the mind quickly returns to its usual level of contentment. A phone bought after a month of comparing is, a month later, simply a phone.

There is a fourth cost, the least visible one: fatigue. The mind gets tired from deciding the way the body gets tired from lifting, and from the moment we wake we use it up on third-rate matters: what to wear, what to eat, what to watch, what to answer first. Researchers call this decision fatigue and point to its effects: toward evening, after hundreds of micro-choices, we become more prone to impulsive decisions or to putting everything off until later. It’s no accident that some well-known people wore the same outfit every day: not out of poverty, but so as not to spend their morning store of attention on something that doesn’t matter. The practical takeaway is simple: put the small stuff on autopilot. A set menu for the week, a set shopping list, a set time and route for your walk. Every such routine wins back a portion of decision-making strength for the things that truly need it.

Researchers who study choice have described two kinds of people. The maximizer has to have the best possible option: looking through everything, comparing, going back, checking once more. The satisficer settles in advance on what they need and takes the first thing that meets those conditions. The findings are counterintuitive: objectively, maximizers choose slightly better, but subjectively they are clearly less satisfied with their choices, have more regrets, and torment themselves more often. So “good enough” isn’t surrender. It’s the wisdom of people who have understood that a decision is meant to serve life, not life to serve the decision. You can see this painfully where the stakes are highest: in choosing a person to spend your life with. The age of endlessly scrolling through candidates whispers that someone better is always one swipe away, and that whisper makes commitment harder for people today than almost anything else. Yet lasting marriages are not the work of people who found the perfect option, but of people who stopped looking for a better one.

What about the decision-making process itself? We make the most common mistake before we even start thinking: we set the question in too narrow a frame. “Change jobs or stay?” “Buy this car or not?” A “whether” question usually hides all the other possibilities: renegotiating your terms at your current job, switching fields, going part-time, a used car, putting the purchase off for a year. A good test goes like this: what would I do if this option didn’t exist at all? If, once both the “yes” and the “no” boxes disappear, you suddenly see three other doors, the frame was too narrow. The second mistake we already know from the traps of the mind: when deep down we lean toward something, we gather only the arguments in favor, so we have to deliberately look for information that could prove us wrong. The third is passing emotion: infatuation, anger, and fear are terrible advisers in matters that will last for years. A simple distance exercise helps: how will I think about this decision in ten days, in ten months, and in ten years? Many things that burn today turn out to be trifles from ten months away, while the weight of others only comes to light then. Switching chairs works in a similar way: ask yourself what you would advise your best friend if they were the one facing this choice. It’s astonishing how much more clearly we see other people’s affairs than our own, and we can draw on that clarity whenever we want. And the fourth mistake: overconfidence that we know how things will turn out. We don’t, so a wise decision leaves a margin: financial, time, and a way back, if possible.

Another very practical rule is that there are two kinds of decisions. Reversible ones, the kind you can back out of, should be made quickly and cheaply, because the cost of a possible mistake is small while the cost of endless hesitation is large. Irreversible ones, such as marriage, selling a house, or leaving a profession, should be made slowly, with reflection, counsel, and a safety margin. Most people do exactly the opposite: they spend weeks choosing a TV and take life’s major turns on momentum. It also helps to set your criteria before looking at options, because whoever looks first lets advertising write their criteria. We also need to call out the favorite hiding place of us all: procrastination. A decision not made is still a decision, only one made by circumstances, and usually the most expensive one there is, because putting things off runs a quiet meter: months in a job that burns you out, years in limbo that nobody agreed to. Researchers who ask people at the end of life about their regrets, by the way, hear something instructive: older people rarely regret the decisions they made, even the ones that missed the mark, but often regret the ones they never made at all. We can make peace with a mistake over time; with “I never tried” it is much harder. And one underrated point: once you’ve decided, stop comparing. The satisficer closes the door behind them and gets on with living; the maximizer spends another year looking over their shoulder to see whether the other option wasn’t better, and that looking back costs more than the decision itself.

Finally, the most important thing, though it sounds the least technical: a compass. A huge part of our decision fatigue comes from deciding every matter separately, from zero, as though a war over values had to be fought all over again each time. A person who has settled once and for all what matters most to them, for example that family comes before career and honesty before comfort, discovers that most decisions make themselves. They don’t have to debate every evening whether to stay for a third hour of overtime, because they made that decision once, at the level of values, and the evenings simply carry it out. A compass doesn’t excuse you from thinking, but it lifts hundreds of recurring dilemmas off your shoulders.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: Too many options don’t set us free; they paralyze us and rob us of joy in what we chose: with twenty-four jams people buy ten times less often than with six. So choose like a pro: set your criteria in advance, take the first option that meets them, and don’t compare after you’ve decided. Put the small stuff on autopilot, because the mind gets tired from deciding and by evening may run short for what matters. In important matters, widen the frame by asking, “What would I do if this option didn’t exist?”, look for arguments against your own leaning, test the choice at a distance of ten days, months, and years, ask what you would advise a friend, and leave a margin for error. Make reversible decisions quickly and irreversible ones slowly. And a compass of values, settled once, will lift the most decisions off your shoulders.

sections.heading: Look Higher
paragraphs: When young Solomon took the throne, he heard a question in a vision by night: what did he want to ask for? He didn’t ask for riches or a long life, but for an understanding heart, able to discern between good and evil. The Bible calls this ability wisdom and treats it not as a talent but as a gift we are free to ask for: whoever feels they lack it should ask God, who gives generously and without finding fault. That takes the loneliness out of deciding. The book of Proverbs adds a line everyone who makes plans knows well: a man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps. Our part is to weigh things honestly; His part is to lead us on from there, even when we didn’t choose the best. Hence the old practice of people of faith of bringing important decisions to prayer first: not to avoid thinking, but to think in the presence of Someone who sees farther down the road than we do. “Commit your works to the LORD and your plans will be achieved,” the same book of Proverbs promises. Because this, too, is part of the good news: a person’s worth doesn’t depend on how well they choose. Whoever knows this decides with a calmer heart.

quote.text: Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him.

questions: Which unmade decision has been hanging over you the longest, and what is putting it off really costing you?
Do you have a compass of values, settled once, that decides most matters for you, or do you decide every matter from scratch?
What would you ask for if God asked you tonight, as He asked Solomon?
